\chapter{Numbers 11–20 and Weather}
\label{ch:ka-numbers-and-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what the weather is doing in Kannada and count past ten up to twenty.}

Say \kn{ಹವಾಮಾನ} — the Persian hava plus Sanskrit māna — and report the weather with \kn{ಮಳೆ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ}, \textquotedblleft{}rain is coming.\textquotedblright{}
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದು} — \kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು}]{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದು} to \kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು} — numbers 11–20}

\label{lesson:KA-C20-hannondu-ippattu}



\begin{quote}
You've now seen four different language families each build \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{} as its own special, opaque word — Sanskrit's \emph{vimshati}, Latin's \emph{viginti}, Arabic's \emph{ʿishrūn}. Kannada's twenty genuinely started life as \textquotedblleft{}two tens\textquotedblright{} too — but be careful: the modern surface no longer shows it plainly.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Kannada's teens are built on \textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತು}} (\emph{hattu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) plus each digit — \textbf{\kn{ಹನ್ನೊಂದು}} (\emph{hannondu}, 11), \textbf{\kn{ಹನ್ನೆರಡು}} (\emph{hanneraḍu}, 12), and onward through \textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತೊಂಬತ್ತು}} (\emph{hattombattu}, 19). Each teen is a compound built the same way English builds \textquotedblleft{}four-\textbf{teen}\textquotedblright{} — just placed the same digit-plus-ten pattern in front instead of behind.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು}} (\emph{ippattu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{twenty}\textquotedblright{}) traces back to Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*ir-} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two}\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{*paHtu} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) — a genuine compositional origin, \textquotedblleft{}two-tens.\textquotedblright{} But be honest about what's actually visible today: the \textbf{*ir-} piece is an old \emph{bound} root, not the same as modern Kannada's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}two,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} (\emph{eraḍu}) — a separate, longer descendant of the same ancient family. And the \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} piece surfaces here as \textbf{-pp-} (geminated after the \emph{r}), not as modern \textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತು}} (\emph{hattu})'s \textbf{h-} — because Kannada's historical \emph{p $\to$ h} shift only fired at the \textbf{start} of a word, and this \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} sits in the \textbf{middle} of the compound, so it never lenited. So \emph{ippattu} really did start as \textquotedblleft{}two-tens\textquotedblright{} — you just can't spot modern \emph{eraḍu} or modern \emph{hattu} inside it anymore the way you might expect. Compare this to Sanskrit's \textbf{\dv{विंशति}} (\emph{vimshati}), Latin's \textbf{vīgintī}, and Arabic's \textbf{\ar{عشرون}} (\emph{ʿishrūn}): those have \textbf{no} compositional \textquotedblleft{}two-ten\textquotedblright{} origin at all, not even a buried one — a genuinely different kind of history from Kannada's.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hannondu, hanneraḍu\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hattu\textquotedblright{} — ten (today's word), \textquotedblleft{}eraḍu\textquotedblright{} — two (today's word)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ippattu\textquotedblright{} — twenty, \textquotedblleft{}two-tens\textquotedblright{} underneath, from the OLD \emph{ir-/ }paHtu roots, not directly from hattu/eraḍu
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How are Kannada's teens built? (\textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತು}} (ten) + a digit, compounded.) Does \textbf{\kn{ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು}} (twenty) have a compositional \textquotedblleft{}two-tens\textquotedblright{} origin? (\textbf{Yes} — Proto-Dravidian \emph{*ir-} \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} + \emph{*paHtu} \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{}) Can you still spot modern \emph{eraḍu} or modern \emph{hattu} inside it today? (\textbf{No} — the old bound \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} root and the un-lenited middle-of-word \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} root look different from their modern standalone descendants.) Do Sanskrit's \emph{vimshati} or Latin's \emph{vīgintī} have any compositional origin like this at all? (\textbf{No} — neither has a buried \textquotedblleft{}two-ten\textquotedblright{} history the way Kannada's does.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[havāmāna]{\kn{ಹವಾಮಾನ} — a genuine two-language hybrid word}

\label{lesson:KA-C20-havamana}



\begin{quote}
Kannada's word for \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} isn't purely Sanskrit or purely native — it's a compound with a piece from each of two different borrowed sources.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹವಾಮಾನ}} (\emph{havāmāna}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — built from two pieces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹವಾ}} (\emph{hava}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{air}\textquotedblright{}) — itself a loanword, from \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{هوا}} (\emph{havā}), which traces back to \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{هَوَاء}} (\emph{hawāʾ}, \textquotedblleft{}air\textquotedblright{}). This is the exact same root behind Hindi's own \textbf{\dv{हवा}} (\emph{havā}, \textquotedblleft{}air, wind\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮಾನ}} (\emph{māna}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{measure}\textquotedblright{}) — from \textbf{Sanskrit} \textbf{\dv{मान}} (\emph{māna}), \textquotedblleft{}measure, standard\textquotedblright{} (the same word behind \emph{pramāṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}proof, measure of truth\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{havāmāna} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{air-measure}\textquotedblright{} — and it's genuinely a two-source hybrid, not a single borrowed compound: one piece Perso-Arabic, one piece Sanskrit, fused into one Kannada word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮಳೆ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ} — \textquotedblleft{}rain is coming\textquotedblright{}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಮಳೆ} \kn{ಬರುತ್ತಿದೆ}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rain is coming}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{maḷe baruttide.})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}havāmāna\textquotedblright{} — weather, literally \textquotedblleft{}air-measure\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hava\textquotedblright{} — air, a Persian/Arabic loan
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maḷe baruttide\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, \textquotedblleft{}rain is coming\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \textbf{\kn{ಹವಾಮಾನ}}, and where does each come from? (\textbf{\kn{ಹವಾ}}, \textquotedblleft{}air,\textquotedblright{} a \textbf{Persian/Arabic} loan; \textbf{\kn{ಮಾನ}}, \textquotedblleft{}measure,\textquotedblright{} native \textbf{Sanskrit}.) What does \emph{havāmāna} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Air-measure}.\textquotedblright{}) What other Indian language shares the exact same word for \textquotedblleft{}air\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Hindi} — \emph{havā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pa]{\kn{ಪ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S124-letter-pa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌ಂ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಪ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಪ}} — \emph{pa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{p}, it is \textbf{pa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಪ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ}} \emph{paravāgilla} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕಪ್ಪು} \kn{ಬಿಳಿ} \kn{ಕೆಂಪು} \kn{ನೀಲಿ}} — black, white, red, blue
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಪ್ಪ} \kn{ಅಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಅಣ್ಣ} \kn{ತಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಅಕ್ಕ} \kn{ತಂಗಿ}} — father, mother, and four age-graded sibling words
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಚೈತ್ರ} \kn{ವೈಶಾಖ} \kn{ಜ್ಯೇಷ್ಠ} \kn{ಆಷಾಢ} \kn{ಶ್ರಾವಣ} \kn{ಭಾದ್ರಪದ} \kn{ಆಶ್ವಯುಜ} \kn{ಕಾರ್ತೀಕ} \kn{ಮಾರ್ಗಶಿರ} \kn{ಪುಷ್ಯ} \kn{ಮಾಘ} \kn{ಫಾಲ್ಗುಣ}} — the twelve lunisolar months
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಪ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಪ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಪ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ}  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಪ} three times, saying \emph{pa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಪ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಪ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{pa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
